                                                   PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

              RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                           §    PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
              LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                        §                 OF TEXAS
              STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                    §
                                                                §
                                                                §

                                    INITIAL COMMENTS OF BKV CORPORATION

                                                    I.       INTRODUCTION

                     BKV Corporation (“BKV”) submits these Initial Comments in response to the
            Commission’s Proposal for Publication (“PFP”) of new 16 TAC § 25.194 implementing large load
            interconnection standards under PURA § 37.0561. BKV owns and operates large, thermal, grid-
            facing generation facilities in the ERCOT region and is actively evaluating co-location structures
            involving large load customers, including configurations in which dispatchable generation
            resources are paired with transmission-voltage load. In parallel, BKV is developing additional
            dispatchable generation resources, the advancement of which is directly influenced by the
            regulatory framework governing large load interconnection, cost allocation, and co-located system
            configurations.

                     BKV supports the Commission’s objective of establishing a standardized, transparent
            framework to ensure that large load interconnection requests reflect credible, financeable projects
            and that cost responsibility is appropriately aligned with system impacts. At the same time, the
            rule must be implemented in a manner that preserves regulatory certainty, adheres to cost-causation
            principles, and does not introduce duplicative or non-cost-based financial burdens that would
            discourage efficient co-location structures or undermine investment incentives for dispatchable
            generation resources that are critical to ERCOT system reliability.

                     PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards that
            support business development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining
            system reliability. Achieving these objectives requires a framework that: (i) aligns financial
            obligations with actual cost incurrence and demonstrable system risk; (ii) preserves reliance
            interests for projects that have advanced under existing interconnection frameworks; and (iii)
            avoids procedural or financial constructs that distort efficient project development or deter


                                                                1
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




            investment in integrated generation-load configurations.

                     PURA § 37.0561 provides the Commission with authority to establish interconnection
            standards, but that authority is bounded by the statute’s express objectives and by fundamental
            cost-causation principles. While the statute directs the Commission to support business
            development and minimize stranded infrastructure costs, it does not support the imposition of
            financial requirements that are not tied to identifiable, project-specific cost exposure, nor does it
            permit the reallocation of costs that have already been assigned and funded under existing
            interconnection frameworks. Likewise, nothing in the statute contemplates the retroactive
            application of new financial or procedural requirements to projects that have already satisfied
            applicable interconnection obligations. Any interpretation or implementation of the proposed rule
            that extends beyond these parameters risks exceeding the Commission’s statutory authority and
            introducing regulatory uncertainty that undermines the investment signals SB 6 was intended to
            preserve.

                              II.     PROSPECTIVE APPLICATION AND PROTECTION
                                            OF RELIANCE INTERESTS

                     The proposed rule, as drafted, does not include a clear statement of prospective application.
            This omission could be interpreted to impose new financial, procedural, or study-related
            requirements on projects that have already executed interconnection agreements, except to the
            limited extent necessary to address incremental facilities, system impacts, or cost exposure not
            previously studied, assigned, or secured.

                     This concern is not theoretical. As reflected in various stakeholder comments in this
            rulemaking, the absence of a global applicability provision leaves open the possibility that “in-
            flight” or advanced-stage projects—particularly co-located configurations governed by executed
            standard generation interconnection agreements (“SGIA”)— could be subject to re-evaluation, re-
            screening, or duplicative financial obligations with respect to facilities, studies, or system impacts
            that have already been reviewed and funded under prior interconnection frameworks.

                     For generation owners evaluating co-location structures, this uncertainty directly affects
            investment decisions. Generation-side interconnection facilities, system upgrades, and associated
            financial security and/or contributions in aid of construction (“CIAC”) are often developed and
            funded under SGIAs that contemplate both generation and load integration at a shared point of

                                                               2
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




            interconnection (“POI”). Re-opening those determinations or imposing additional requirements ex
            post would undermine regulatory certainty, impair reliance interests, and create a material
            disincentive to pursue integrated and bring-your-own-generation (“BYOG”) configurations.

                     Absent this clarification, application of § 25.194 to projects that have already executed
            governing interconnection agreements, completed required studies, and funded interconnection
            facilities would operate as a retroactive reallocation of cost responsibility and project requirements,
            rather than a forward-looking application limited to new or incremental system impacts. Such an
            outcome is not supported by PURA § 37.0561, which applies to new or expanded interconnection
            requests, and would be inconsistent with longstanding Texas law disfavoring retroactive regulatory
            imposition absent clear legislative authorization. Accordingly, any application of § 25.194 to
            existing projects should be expressly limited to incremental facilities or system impacts not
            previously studied or assigned, and structured as a narrowly tailored true-up mechanism tied to
            demonstrable cost exposure rather than a re-underwriting of prior determinations.

                     This clarification is particularly important in the context of co-located configurations,
            where the governing interconnection agreement—often an SGIA—may be executed by a
            generation entity but encompasses the interconnection facilities, studies, and system impacts
            associated with both generation and any co-located load served at a common POI. In such cases,
            the relevant inquiry is not the identity of the executing entity, but whether the applicable facilities
            and system impacts have already been studied, approved, and financially secured.

                                     III.    CREDITABLE AND NON-DUPLICATIVE
                                               FINANCIAL FRAMEWORK

                     The financial framework proposed in § 25.194 introduces multiple layers of obligations,
            including intermediate agreement security, a non-refundable interconnection fee, CIAC, financial
            security for equipment and services, and separate security for system upgrades. Absent explicit
            crediting and coordination, this structure creates a substantial risk of overlapping or duplicative
            financial requirements applied to the same underlying facilities or cost components, particularly
            where multiple forms of security or payment are required to be posted concurrently without
            explicit crediting.




                                                              3
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




                     As structured, this framework risks exceeding what is permissible under PURA § 35.004
            and § 37.0561 by imposing layered financial obligations that are not clearly tied to distinct, non-
            overlapping cost components or differentiated categories of stranded cost risk. The Commission’s
            authority to require financial commitments is limited to ensuring that a large load customer
            contributes to the recovery of costs caused by its interconnection. It does not extend to requiring
            multiple forms of financial assurance for the same underlying facilities or to establishing
            standardized financial thresholds that are not calibrated to project-specific cost exposure.

                     This outcome is inconsistent with cost-causation principles embedded in PURA § 35.004
            and § 37.0561, which require that cost recovery be tied to actual system costs and the customer-
            specific impacts that give rise to those costs. It also introduces capital inefficiencies that do not
            enhance reliability or reduce stranded cost risk, and contradicts the statute’s co-equal directive to
            support business development.

                     BKV supports a unified, creditable financial structure to the maximum extent practicable,
            recognizing that certain categories—such as system upgrade security tied to demonstrable stranded
            cost risk—may remain distinct but should not be duplicative. The absence of such crediting is ripe
            for “double collateralization,” which will inherently include unnecessary capital burdens without
            providing incremental system protection.

                     Under a properly structured framework:

                         1. Intermediate-stage security should be released when security is posted under an
                            Interconnection Agreement, unless the customer elects to carry it forward for other
                            financial obligations;

                         2. CIAC and equipment-related payments should be fully creditable and not
                            duplicative of other security requirements;

                         3. Additional financial obligations should be limited to incremental, project-specific
                            costs not already secured or funded; and

                         4. To the extent multiple financial instruments are retained, the rule should expressly
                            require transparent accounting and appropriate crediting across categories,
                            including dollar-for-dollar crediting where obligations correspond to the same
                            underlying facilities or cost components, to prevent overlapping collateralization of
                            the same cost exposure.

                     Without explicit crediting and coordination, these provisions result in over-securitization
            of interconnection-related costs, increasing the cost of capital without corresponding protection

                                                              4
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




            against stranded infrastructure and effectively shifting financial responsibility beyond the large
            load’s actual system impact. While system upgrade security may remain distinct where tied to
            demonstrable stranded cost risk, it should be limited to actual upgrade scope and not imposed on
            a standardized or duplicative basis.

                                IV.     NON-REFUNDABLE INTERCONNECTION FEE

                     The proposed non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000/MW is not supported by cost
            causation principles to the extent it is not tied to identifiable, project-specific costs or demonstrable
            stranded cost risk. Unlike CIAC or security for equipment and services, which correspond to
            discrete, project-specific costs, the fee operates as a standardized charge that is imposed without
            regard to whether corresponding costs are incurred, duplicating or exceeding amounts already
            secured through other mechanisms.

                     In practice, this construct would function as a penalty-like or deterrent mechanism rather
            than a cost recovery tool where it is not credited against actual interconnection-related
            expenditures, and particularly in circumstances where:

                         1. Interconnection facilities have already been funded through SGIA-based CIAC;

                         2. System upgrades are fully secured through other mechanisms; or

                         3. The large load’s incremental impact on the system is limited or already reflected in
                            prior studies.

            For generation owners evaluating co-location, the imposition of a non-refundable fee on top of
            existing generation-funded infrastructure materially distorts the economics of integrated
            configurations and discourages efficient use of existing interconnection capacity.

                     As a result, the fee functions as a non-cost-based exaction rather than a cost recovery tool,
            and risks operating as a penalty for interconnection rather than a mechanism to mitigate stranded
            infrastructure risk. This exceeds the scope of the Commission’s authority under PURA § 35.004
            and § 37.0561, both of which are grounded in cost recovery—not revenue generation or deterrence.

                     Accordingly, the Commission should, at a minimum, modify the non-refundable fee
            construct to ensure that it is either (i) fully creditable toward actual interconnection-related costs,
            or (ii) limited to a narrowly defined, non-refundable component demonstrably tied to
            administrative or early-stage costs that are not otherwise recoverable.

                                                               5
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




              V.       RECOGNITION OF CO-LOCATED AND INTEGRATED CONFIGURATIONS

                     As drafted, § 25.194 does not adequately account for integrated configurations in which
            large load is co-located with generation at a common POI, including behind-the-meter (“BTM”)
            arrangements and private use networks (“PUNs”).

                     In these configurations, substantial infrastructure investment is often made under an SGIA
            that governs the interconnection facilities, studies, and system upgrades required to support both
            generation and load. Planning Guide § 9.5.2 expressly contemplates that co-located configurations
            may be governed by an SGIA and, in certain circumstances, may not require additional
            interconnection agreements.

                     Absent explicit recognition of this framework, § 25.194 creates a material risk that large
            load customers could be required to post additional financial security for facilities or capacity that
            have already been studied, assigned, and funded under an SGIA or equivalent construct at the same
            point of interconnection.

                     Requiring additional financial security in these circumstances would result in duplicative
            recovery of the same interconnection-related costs, contrary to fundamental ratemaking principles
            and the Commission’s obligation to ensure that charges reflect only those costs caused by the
            requesting customer. The rule should not be interpreted to permit multiple recovery of the same
            facilities or upgrades simply because the load and generation components are structured through
            separate legal entities.

                     The Commission should therefore clarify that:

                         1. Where interconnection facilities and upgrades have been funded or secured under
                            an executed SGIA, those investments are credited toward any obligations under §
                            25.194 to the extent they correspond to the same facilities or capacity;

                         2. Financial obligations under § 25.194 are limited to incremental facilities and system
                            impacts attributable to the large load; and

                         3. No additional security or CIAC is required for facilities that do not give rise to new
                            or increased system upgrade costs.

                     For the avoidance of doubt, the relevant inquiry should be whether the facilities, upgrades,
            and system impacts at issue have already been evaluated and funded—not the contractual form or
            identity of the executing entity—such that duplicative financial requirements are not imposed

                                                               6
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




            based solely on project. This clarification is essential to preserve efficient co-location structures
            that pair dispatchable generation with large loads and enhance system reliability.

                       VI.      INTERMEDIATE AGREEMENT AND STUDY PROGRESSION

                     The intermediate agreement requirement should function as a mechanism to establish
            project credibility and enable timely initiation of interconnection studies. For existing grid-facing
            generation seeking to co-locate with large load, the intermediate agreement should operate as a
            limited, administrative mechanism to confirm load-side readiness and enable timely progression
            of studies that build upon an already-established interconnection framework.

                     However, as drafted, § 25.194(d) introduces a risk that the intermediate agreement could
            be interpreted or applied in combination with financial commitment and site control requirements
            in combination with financial commitment and site control requirements as a gating construct that
            delays study initiation beyond what is necessary to establish baseline project viability. In the co-
            location context, this risk is heightened where such requirements are applied notwithstanding the
            existence of an executed SGIA, completed generation-side studies, and established system
            impacts. This risk is heightened where intermediate agreement requirements are not expressly
            limited to objective, rule-based criteria and could be expanded through utility-specific practices.

                     Such an interpretation would be inconsistent with ERCOT Planning Guide § 9, which
            establishes a sequencing framework in which studies inform planning and should not be delayed
            by non-essential prerequisites. In the co-location context, where generation is already
            interconnected or has satisfied prior interim interconnection requirements or current Planning
            Guide requirements, imposing additional gating requirements on the load side risks re-opening or
            effectively re-underwriting previously completed studies. Delays in study initiation in this context
            impair the ability to synchronize generation and load development, introduce restudy risk, and
            increase project risk cost without corresponding reliability benefits.

                     The proposed batch study process presents regulatory uncertainty and potential delay for
            projects fulfilling all statutory requirements for a net metering study under SB 6. This concern is
            particularly acute for co-located configurations where generation-side impacts have already been
            studied and funded. Despite compliance, ERCOT may disqualify a large load customer with a co-
            located generation resource from consideration as firm load in Batch Zero if its studies are deemed


                                                             7
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




            deficient under evolving or case-by-case study validity criteria. Further, it may be excluded the
            initial batch altogether, delaying approval for years, as ERCOT’s proposed revalidation of studies
            against current system conditions introduces uncertainty and may result in deferral to a subsequent
            batch cycle. As a result, integrated projects may be deferred despite having satisfied all material
            readiness requirements and without any demonstrated incremental system impact beyond that
            already studied.

                     The command of § 37.0561(b) to support business development and considerations of
            fairness and equity support recognition of a separate pathway governed by SB 6 for co-located
            generation and load configurations with established interconnection status for those entities
            complying with the letter of the law before batch study implementation. Where generation facilities
            have already satisfied interconnection requirements and funded necessary infrastructure,
            duplicative study requirements are not necessary to achieve reliability objectives.

                     Accordingly, the Commission should clarify that:

                         1. The intermediate agreement is a threshold requirement limited to objective
                            indicators of project readiness and, for co-located projects, is limited to load-side
                            readiness and does not reopen or condition generation-side interconnection status;

                         2. Utilities may not impose additional conditions that delay study initiation beyond
                            those specified in the rule, particularly where the underlying generation
                            interconnection has been completed and/or satisfied the applicable large load
                            interconnection requirements effective at that time;

                         3. Study initiation and progression must be aligned with ERCOT-established
                            processes, including modeling readiness and validation requirements, and for co-
                            located load must build on existing modeling assumptions and prior study results,
                            with any additional analysis limited to incremental load-related impacts; and

                         4. Entities that have fulfilled the requirements of SB 6 before batch study
                            implementation shall be permitted to proceed without re-screening under the
                            subsequently adopted eligibility criteria, and co-located projects with existing or
                            approved grid-facing generation shall not be subject to revalidation, displacement,
                            or re-underwriting of previously completed studies.

                     VII.     FINANCIAL SECURITY, WITHDRAWAL, AND PROPORTIONAL
                                            RISK ALLOCATION

                     The provisions governing withdrawal, milestone compliance, and financial security release
            must be calibrated to reflect actual cost exposure and system risk. As drafted, the rule creates a

                                                              8
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




            risk creates that financial security could be forfeited or retained in excess of the amount necessary
            to recover non-recoverable or irrevocably committed costs directly attributable to the project. To
            the extent the rule directs any remaining balance of financial security to rate base or other purposes
            absent a demonstrated nexus to stranded infrastructure costs, it risks exceeding a cost-recovery
            framework and should be clarified or limited accordingly

                     Financial security should function as a targeted risk mitigation tool, not as a punitive or
            revenue-generating mechanism. To the extent financial security is forfeited or retained beyond the
            amount necessary to recover non-recoverable or irrevocably committed costs, the mechanism
            ceases to function as cost protection and instead operates as a penalty. Nothing in PURA § 37.0561
            authorizes the Commission to impose penalty-based financial constructs in the interconnection
            context, and such an approach would be inconsistent with the statutory objective of minimizing
            stranded infrastructure costs rather than imposing punitive financial consequences.

                     Accordingly, forfeiture should be limited to documented, non-recoverable or irrevocably
            committed costs directly attributable to the project, and any remaining security should be promptly
            released once underlying cost exposure has been satisfied, rather than on fixed timelines that do
            not correspond to actual system risk.

                     Milestone and energization requirements should also account for the practical realities of
            large-scale development, including phased buildouts, supply chain constraints, and coordination
            with generation development in co-located configurations, and should not result in forfeiture or
            delay where the underlying system risk remains appropriately mitigated.

                                 VIII. ALIGNMENT WITH ERCOT PLANNING AND
                                           MARKET DEVELOPMENT

                     Alignment between § 25.194 and ERCOT planning processes, including PGRR 145 and
            the Batch Zero framework, is essential to avoid duplicative requirements and inconsistent
            treatment of projects. Misalignment between Commission rules and ERCOT processes creates a
            risk of re-screening, reclassification, or loss of study position for projects that have otherwise
            satisfied applicable readiness, study, and financial commitment criteria under either § 25.194 or
            ERCOT Planning Guide processes. The Commission should seek to ensure consistency in
            underlying criteria and definitions, while recognizing that ERCOT retains responsibility for
            implementation of planning and study processes.

                                                              9
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




                     In addition, the Commission should ensure that the rule does not preempt or conflict with
            ongoing ERCOT stakeholder efforts to develop frameworks for controllable load resources,
            BYOG configurations, and related constructs. These developments are central to integrating large
            loads in a manner that enhances system reliability and supports efficient market outcomes.

                     Concurrently, the Commission should not passively accept ERCOT’s BYOG and batching
            framework as its own in this rulemaking without due consideration. While the constructs should
            be aligned, the Commission has an obligation to ensure that such constructs are consistent with
            statutory requirements, Commission policy objectives, and principles of fairness, cost causation,
            and reliability.

                     For generation owners like BKV, the regulatory treatment of co-located large load is not a
            discrete issue—it directly affects the economic viability of new dispatchable generation
            development. Frameworks that introduce duplicative cost exposure, uncertainty in interconnection
            treatment, or misalignment between cost responsibility and system benefit will discourage
            investment in precisely the types of resources—dispatchable, grid-facing generation—that
            ERCOT requires to maintain reliability under increasing load growth. At the same time, properly
            structured frameworks enable co-located load to be supported by dispatchable resources that can
            respond to system conditions, reducing net load variability and improving reliability outcomes.
            The rule should therefore be calibrated not only to manage large load risk, but to preserve and
            support continued investment in dispatchable generation resources.

                                                     IX.     CONCLUSION

                     BKV supports the Commission’s objective of establishing a clear and durable large load
            interconnection framework under PURA § 37.0561. However, as currently drafted, § 25.194
            introduces material risks related to retroactive application, duplicative financial obligations, and
            misalignment with integrated project configurations.

                     With targeted revisions—specifically, explicit prospective application limited to
            incremental impacts, strengthened anti-duplication and crediting provisions within the financial
            framework, refinement (rather than elimination) of non-cost-based fee constructs, recognition of
            SGIA-governed co-location structures, and alignment with ERCOT planning processes—the rule
            can achieve its statutory objectives while preserving the investment signals necessary to support


                                                               10
 Docusign Envelope ID: D7D1B261-531D-843A-81C7-E30ACF94C608




            both large load development and continued investment in dispatchable generation resources that
            are essential to ERCOT system reliability.




            Date: April 17, 2026                                  Respectfully submitted,



                                                                   /s/
                                                                  Lindsay Larrick
                                                                  Chief Legal Officer
                                                                  BKV Corporation
                                                                  lindsaylarrick@bkvcorp.com

                                                   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

               Statutory Limits / Cost Causation
                   o PURA § 37.0561 requires cost causation-based recovery; the rule should not impose
                       duplicative or non-cost-based financial obligations or reallocate previously assigned costs.

               Prospective Application
                   o Limit application to incremental facilities and system impacts; prohibit re-underwriting of
                      projects with executed agreements, completed studies, and funded infrastructure.

               Financial Framework
                   o Prevent overlapping financial requirements across security, CIAC, and fees.
                   o Require crediting across instruments where tied to the same facilities or cost components.
                   o Limit obligations to incremental, project-specific costs.

               Non-Refundable Fee
                  o Modify to ensure cost-based justification; at minimum, make creditable or narrowly tied to
                     non-recoverable administrative costs.

               Co-Located Configurations (BTM / PUN / BYOG)
                   o Credit SGIA-funded infrastructure; prohibit duplicative recovery.
                   o Focus on facilities and impacts at the POI, not entity structure.

               Intermediate Agreement
                   o Clarify as non-discretionary, threshold requirement; cannot delay study initiation beyond
                      rule-based criteria.

               Financial Security / Forfeiture
                   o Limit forfeiture to documented, non-recoverable costs.
                   o Require release of excess security once risk is satisfied.
                   o Avoid penalty-like retention not tied to stranded cost recovery.

               ERCOT Alignment
                  o Align with Planning Guide and PGRR 145; avoid re-screening or reclassification of
                    advanced projects.
                  o Preserve flexibility for evolving BYOG / controllable load frameworks.

               Reliability and Investment Signal
                   o Avoid duplicative cost exposure that discourages dispatchable generation investment.
                   o Enable co-location to support reliability through dispatchable resources.

               Additional Refinements
                  o Refine the rule to ensure incremental cost responsibility, creditable financial structures, and
                       recognition of co-located configurations, consistent with statutory objectives.

                                         III.      CREDITABLE AND NON-DUPLICATIVE
                                                     FINANCIAL FRAMEWORK

                       The financial framework proposed in § 25.194 introduces multiple layers of obligations,
              including intermediate agreement security, a non-refundable interconnection fee, CIAC, financial
              security for equipment and services, and separate security for system upgrades. Absent explicit
              crediting and coordination, this structure creates a substantial risk of overlapping or duplicative
              financial requirements applied to the same underlying facilities or cost components, particularly
              where multiple forms of security or payment are required to be posted concurrently without
              explicit crediting.

                       As structured, this framework risks exceeding what is permissible under PURA § 35.004
              and § 37.0561 by imposing layered financial obligations that are not clearly tied to distinct, non-
              overlapping cost components or differentiated categories of stranded cost risk. The Commission's
              authority to require financial commitments is limited to ensuring that a large load customer
              contributes to the recovery of costs caused by its interconnection. It does not extend to requiring
              multiple forms of financial assurance for the same underlying facilities or to establishing
              standardized financial thresholds that are not calibrated to project-specific cost exposure.

                       This outcome is inconsistent with cost-causation principles embedded in PURA § 35.004
              and § 37.0561, which require that cost recovery be tied to actual system costs and the customer-
              specific impacts that give rise to those costs. It also introduces capital inefficiencies that do not
              enhance reliability or reduce stranded cost risk, and contradicts the statute's co-equal directive to
              support business development.

                       BKV supports a unified, creditable financial structure to the maximum extent practicable,
              recognizing that certain categories-such as system upgrade security tied to demonstrable stranded
              cost risk-may remain distinct but should not be duplicative. The absence of such crediting is ripe
              for "double collateralization," which will inherently include unnecessary capital burdens without
              providing incremental system protection.

                       Under a properly structured framework:

                            1. Intermediate-stage security should be released when security is posted under an
                               Interconnection Agreement, unless the customer elects to carry it forward for other
                                 financial obligations;

                            2. CIAC and equipment-related payments should be fully creditable and not
                                 duplicative of other security requirements;

                            3. Additional financial obligations should be limited to incremental, project-specific
                                 costs not already secured or funded; and

                            4. To the extent multiple financial instruments are retained, the rule should expressly
                                 require transparent accounting and appropriate crediting across categories,
                                 including dollar-for-dollar crediting where obligations correspond to the same
                                 underlying facilities or cost components, to prevent overlapping collateralization of
                                 the same cost exposure.

                       Without explicit crediting and coordination, these provisions result in over-securitization
              of interconnection-related costs, increasing the cost of capital without corresponding protection

              against stranded infrastructure and effectively shifting financial responsibility beyond the large
              load's actual system impact. While system upgrade security may remain distinct where tied to
              demonstrable stranded cost risk, it should be limited to actual upgrade scope and not imposed on
              a standardized or duplicative basis.

                                    IV.      NON-REFUNDABLE INTERCONNECTION FEE

                       The proposed non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000/MW is not supported by cost
              causation principles to the extent it is not tied to identifiable, proj ect-specific costs or demonstrable
              stranded cost risk. Unlike CIAC or security for equipment and services, which correspond to
              discrete, project-specific costs, the fee operates as a standardized charge that is imposed without
              regard to whether corresponding costs are incurred, duplicating or exceeding amounts already
              secured through other mechanisms.

                       In practice, this construct would function as a penalty-like or deterrent mechanism rather
              than a cost recovery tool where it is not credited against actual interconnection-related
              expenditures, and particularly in circumstances where:

                            1. Interconnection facilities have already been funded through SGIA-based CIAC;

                            2. System upgrades are fully secured through other mechanisms; or

                            3. The large load's incremental impact on the system is limited or already reflected in
                                 prior studies.

              For generation owners evaluating co-location, the imposition of a non-refundable fee on top of
              existing generation-funded infrastructure materially distorts the economics of integrated
              configurations and discourages efficient use of existing interconnection capacity.

                       As a result, the fee functions as a non-cost-based exaction rather than a cost recovery tool,
              and risks operating as a penalty for interconnection rather than a mechanism to mitigate stranded
              infrastructure risk. This exceeds the scope of the Commission's authority under PURA § 35.004
              and § 37.0561, both ofwhich are grounded in cost recovery-not revenue generation or deterrence.

                       Accordingly, the Commission should, at a minimum, modify the non-refundable fee
              construct to ensure that it is either (i) fully creditable toward actual interconnection-related costs,
              or (ii) limited to a narrowly defined, non-refundable component demonstrably tied to
              administrative or early-stage costs that are not otherwise recoverable.

                V.       RECOGNITION OF CO-LOCATED AND INTEGRATED CONFIGURATIONS

                       As drafted, § 25.194 does not adequately account for integrated configurations in which
              large load is co-located with generation at a common POI, including behind-the-meter ("BTM')
              arrangements and private use networks ("PUNs").

                       In these configurations, substantial infrastructure investment is often made under an SGIA
              that governs the interconnection facilities, studies, and system upgrades required to support both
              generation and load. Planning Guide § 9.5.2 expressly contemplates that co-located configurations
              may be governed by an SGIA and, in certain circumstances, may not require additional
              interconnection agreements.

                       Absent explicit recognition of this framework, § 25.194 creates a material risk that large
              load customers could be required to post additional financial security for facilities or capacity that
              have already been studied, assigned, and funded under an SGIA or equivalent construct at the same
              point of interconnection.

                       Requiring additional financial security in these circumstances would result in duplicative
              recovery ofthe same interconnection-related costs, contrary to fundamental ratemaking principles
              and the Commission's obligation to ensure that charges reflect only those costs caused by the
              requesting customer. The rule should not be interpreted to permit multiple recovery of the same
              facilities or upgrades simply because the load and generation components are structured through
              separate legal entities.

                       The Commission should therefore clarify that:

                            1. Where interconnection facilities and upgrades have been funded or secured under
                               an executed SGIA, those investments are credited toward any obligations under §
                                 25.194 to the extent they correspond to the same facilities or capacity;

                            2. Financial obligations under § 25.194 are limited to incremental facilities and system
                                 impacts attributable to the large load; and

                            3. No additional security or CIAC is required for facilities that do not give rise to new
                               or increased system upgrade costs.

                       For the avoidance of doubt, the relevant inquiry should be whether the facilities, upgrades,
              and system impacts at issue have already been evaluated and funded-not the contractual form or
              identity of the executing entity-such that duplicative financial requirements are not imposed

              based solely on project. This clarification is essential to preserve efficient co-location structures
              that pair dispatchable generation with large loads and enhance system reliability.

                          VI.       INTERMEDIATE AGREEMENT AND STUDY PROGRESSION

                       The intermediate agreement requirement should function as a mechanism to establish
              project credibility and enable timely initiation of interconnection studies. For existing grid-facing
              generation seeking to co-locate with large load, the intermediate agreement should operate as a
              limited, administrative mechanism to confirm load-side readiness and enable timely progression
              of studies that build upon an already-established interconnection framework.

                       However, as drafted, § 25. 194(d) introduces a risk that the intermediate agreement could
              be interpreted or applied in combination with financial commitment and site control requirements
              in combination with financial commitment and site control requirements as a gating construct that
              delays study initiation beyond what is necessary to establish baseline project viability. In the co-
              location context, this risk is heightened where such requirements are applied notwithstanding the
              existence of an executed SGIA, completed generation-side studies, and established system
              impacts. This risk is heightened where intermediate agreement requirements are not expressly
              limited to objective, rule-based criteria and could be expanded through utility-specific practices.

                       Such an interpretation would be inconsistent with ERCOT Planning Guide § 9, which
              establishes a sequencing framework in which studies inform planning and should not be delayed
              by non-essential prerequisites. In the co-location context, where generation is already
              interconnected or has satisfied prior interim interconnection requirements or current Planning
              Guide requirements, imposing additional gating requirements on the load side risks re-opening or
              effectively re-underwriting previously completed studies. Delays in study initiation in this context
              impair the ability to synchronize generation and load development, introduce restudy risk, and
              increase project risk cost without corresponding reliability benefits.

                       The proposed batch study process presents regulatory uncertainty and potential delay for
              projects fulfilling all statutory requirements for a net metering study under SB 6. This concern is
              particularly acute for co-located configurations where generation-side impacts have already been
              studied and funded. Despite compliance, ERCOT may disqualify a large load customer with a co-
              located generation resource from consideration as firm load in Batch Zero if its studies are deemed

                       The command of § 37.0561(b) to support business development and considerations of

                                 interconnection requirements effective at that time;

                        VII.     FINANCIAL SECURITY, WITHDRAWAL, AND PROPORTIONAL
                                               RISK ALLOCATION

                       The provisions governing withdrawal, milestone compliance, and financial security release
              must be calibrated to reflect actual cost exposure and system risk. As drafted, the rule creates a

              risk creates that financial security could be forfeited or retained in excess ofthe amount necessary
              to recover non-recoverable or irrevocably committed costs directly attributable to the proj ect. To
              the extent the rule directs any remaining balance of financial security to rate base or other purposes
              absent a demonstrated nexus to stranded infrastructure costs, it risks exceeding a cost-recovery
              framework and should be clarified or limited accordingly

                       Financial security should function as a targeted risk mitigation tool, not as a punitive or
              revenue-generating mechanism. To the extent financial security is forfeited or retained beyond the
              amount necessary to recover non-recoverable or irrevocably committed costs, the mechanism
              ceases to function as cost protection and instead operates as a penalty. Nothing in PURA § 37.0561
              authorizes the Commission to impose penalty-based financial constructs in the interconnection
              context, and such an approach would be inconsistent with the statutory objective of minimizing
              stranded infrastructure costs rather than imposing punitive financial consequences.

                       Accordingly, forfeiture should be limited to documented, non-recoverable or irrevocably
              committed costs directly attributable to the proj ect, and any remaining security should be promptly
              released once underlying cost exposure has been satisfied, rather than on fixed timelines that do
              not correspond to actual system risk.

                       Milestone and energization requirements should also account for the practical realities of
              large-scale development, including phased buildouts, supply chain constraints, and coordination
              with generation development in co-located configurations, and should not result in forfeiture or
              delay where the underlying system risk remains appropriately mitigated.

                                     VIII. ALIGNMENT WITH ERCOT PLANNING AND
                                               MARKET DEVELOPMENT

                       Alignment between § 25.194 and ERCOT planning processes, including PGRR 145 and
              the Batch Zero framework, is essential to avoid duplicative requirements and inconsistent
              treatment of projects. Misalignment between Commission rules and ERCOT processes creates a
              risk of re-screening, reclassification, or loss of study position for projects that have otherwise
              satisfied applicable readiness, study, and financial commitment criteria under either § 25.194 or
              ERCOT Planning Guide processes. The Commission should seek to ensure consistency in
              underlying criteria and definitions, while recognizing that ERCOT retains responsibility for
              implementation of planning and study processes.

                       In addition, the Commission should ensure that the rule does not preempt or conflict with
              ongoing ERCOT stakeholder efforts to develop frameworks for controllable load resources,
              BYOG configurations, and related constructs. These developments are central to integrating large
              loads in a manner that enhances system reliability and supports efficient market outcomes.

                       Concurrently, the Commission should not passively accept ERCOT's BYOG and batching
              framework as its own in this rulemaking without due consideration. While the constructs should
              be aligned, the Commission has an obligation to ensure that such constructs are consistent with
              statutory requirements, Commission policy objectives, and principles of fairness, cost causation,
              and reliability.

                       For generation owners like BKX the regulatory treatment of co-located large load is not a
              discrete issue-it directly affects the economic viability of new dispatchable generation
              development. Frameworks that introduce duplicative cost exposure, uncertainty in interconnection
              treatment, or misalignment between cost responsibility and system benefit will discourage
              investment in precisely the types of resources-dispatchable, grid-facing generation-that
              ERCOT requires to maintain reliability under increasing load growth. At the same time, properly
              structured frameworks enable co-located load to be supported by dispatchable resources that can
              respond to system conditions, reducing net load variability and improving reliability outcomes.
              The rule should therefore be calibrated not only to manage large load risk, but to preserve and
              support continued investment in dispatchable generation resources.

                                                            IX.     CONCLUSION

                       BKV supports the Commission's objective of establishing a clear and durable large load
              interconnection framework under PURA § 37.0561. However, as currently drafted, § 25.194
              introduces material risks related to retroactive application, duplicative financial obligations, and
              misalignment with integrated project configurations.

                       With targeted revisions-specifically,               explicit prospective application limited to
              incremental impacts, strengthened anti-duplication and crediting provisions within the financial
              framework, refinement (rather than elimination) of non-cost-based fee constructs, recognition of
              SGIA-governed co-location structures, and alignment with ERCOT planning processes-the rule
              can achieve its statutory obj ectives while preserving the investment signals necessary to support
